article_text:
T his ludicrous, rabid thriller, shot largely on first-person GoPros, is like Peep Show on PCP. The cumulative effect is of being crammed into a monster-truck tyre and rolled down Mount Everest. It is relentlessly committed to packing the frame with gratuitously entertaining gimmickry, and needlessly annotates the action in pink graffiti – for example, totting up at one point how many people the hero has knocked unconscious with a dildo – so that it borderline qualifies as experimental cinema. Among the many advantages of its perspective is that it helps us buy that John Hannah, 64, is a parkour genius.

Hannah plays Karl Davis – or that is apparently his name, when this amnesiac wakes up to a Hangover-like bombsite of a hotel room. He’s got a banging headache, party detritus is littered everywhere, and there is a dead body in the bathtub. Or perhaps this scenario is Crank inverted; Davis has left a box of pills and a note to self to take one whenever his heart rate gets too elevated. Which of course happens 10 seconds later. A pair of fake police officers arrive to search the room, only for Davis to trounce them with scary efficiency, just as maid Molly (Radha Mitchell), with whom he shacked up the night before, walks through the door.

Director Chee Keong Cheung showed promising kinetic-action chops with last year’s more serious Lagos-set thriller Son of the Soil . But his hyperactivity is constantly in the red here, as the film flips manically between the perspectives of Karl, Molly and Ivan (Tim Fellingham), a Serbian gangster whose dad was in the tub. As the price on Karl’s head rises, there’s hardly any time to register the delirious barrage through the London underworld: parkouring down a multi-storey car park, dodging a machine gun-toting killer-clown DJ, fending off nightclub patrons using only the aforementioned sex toy, a plunger and a stream of his own urine.

It’s kind of glorious. But, unsurprisingly Cheung can’t keep the novelty level up. Once he gets back to the actual plot after the hour mark, the film reverts to less-than-interesting gangland-retribution shtick. Even making allowances for the hypersonic tempo, Cheung also misses opportunities for adding more deft interludes such as the one in which Molly browses patisserie while Karl is scrabbling across rooftops. If nothing else, Bad Day at the Office is an editor’s lesson in the relationship between pacing and the viewing experience: at 111 hyperventilating minutes, it feels about six hours long.

article_text:
Jennifer Lawrence played the “ X-Men ” character Mystique four times on the big screen between 2011 and 2019, and it appears she has no interest whatsoever in slipping back into the mutant’s iconic blue skin. In fact, the Oscar winner’s days of undergoing any extreme makeup and/or prosthetics-driven character transformation are likely over.

“My favorite part of playing Mystique was the stunts,” Lawrence said in a video interview with Allure magazine. “It was so fun to train in that way and learn how to move. I had the same stunt double, Renee Moneymaker, who was Katniss. She is one of my best friends, so that was great. My least favorite part was most certainly the paint.”

When Allure then asked if she would consider doing heavy prosthetic work like Mystique again, Lawrence shot back: “Never say never, but absolutely fucking not. You know how air brushing is very cold? And I am ticklish. I learned how little sleep I can operate on and what can happen to the human mind when you’ve actually reached your breaking point. And patience!”

In a separate interview on the “Call Her Daddy” podcast, Lawrence recalled the difficulty of having to sit in a makeup chair for eight hours during the making of “X-Men: First Class,” which marked her debut as Mystique.

“For ‘First Class,’ it was all body paint and glue. It was eight hours every time and ticklish,” she said. “You’ve had air brushing, right? Imagine two tiny, cold, compressing air brushes all over your body. I am a hero. No one will understand what I went through.”

Lawrence added that even just for her Mystique screen test before she landed the role she had to dye her hair several different colors in one day, from red to brown, black and blonde. The dye ended up permanently damaging her hair.

article_text:
A month ago, Film Comment Editor Devika Girish interviewed John Early on the Podcast about his fantastic first feature, Maddie’s Secret , about a food influencer, played by John, who secretly struggles with bulimia. Even though the two chatted for nearly an hour about the film’s various influences, from TV movies to erotic thrillers, and John’s delicately balanced performance, they had a lot more to talk about. So John and Devika reunited for a Part 2 exclusively for Film Comment paid subscribers. John reflected on how his understanding of his own movie had changed since we last spoke before the release, what it’s been like taking the film on tour throughout the country, the lessons he’s taken away from the film’s occasional detractors, and more.

article_text:
50 artworks from the collection of Charles Greig, a British academic and expert in Indian art, have been donated to the Tate . The collection includes oil paintings, watercolors and miniatures by artists who lived and worked in India during the 18th and 19th centuries.

The museum described the gift as an “entirely philanthropic act,” with Greig donating the works outright and without the use of tax incentives. Greig built the collection over four decades and features artists such as Sita Ram and Ghulam Ali Khan—who capitalized on the new market for their work among British East India Company officials—as well as European artists such as Johan Zoffany and Rudolf Swoboda, and British landscapists like William Hodges, Thomas Daniell and William Daniell. The works in the collection reflect India and Britain’s shared history and complex power dynamics between the two nations.

Greig said in a statement that the main focus of his collection was an exploration of the “deep and intricate relationship between Britain and the Indian subcontinent through the entwined complexities of the artistic encounter. Most of the works were made in the vanished world before photography and they provide us with a visual record of our rich shared history from about 1770.” He called assembling this collection his life’s “primary passion, but at no stage did I ever see myself as other than a temporary steward.”

Notable artworks in the collection include German painter Johan Zoffany’s Portrait of Prince Jawan Bakht (also known as Jahandar Shah) (1784), making it one of only three portraits of individual Indian sitters by the artist to be held in UK public collections; Austrian painter Rudolph Swoboda’s Sepoy in HH Maharaja Srinagar’s Indian Regiment, 23 Years Old (1886), painted for Queen Victoria , is the first work by the artist to enter a British museum collection. The three watercolors by Sita Ram draw on both Indian art traditions and European visual languages.

“These works encompass a unique cross-cultural discourse, it seems to me vital that they are preserved intact to be enjoyed and studied by all mankind. A collection built on a life of study deserves to be universally accessible and I am profoundly happy to see these works find a permanent home at Tate,” said Greig.

The collection is expected to be exhibited at the Tate Britain in 2028. Alex Farquharson , director of Tate Britain, said in a statement that the museum is “always looking to tell new and different stories about Britain’s role in international art history” and that this gift from Greig will “significantly strengthen our holdings of art produced in the British Empire and broaden the range of people and histories represented in the national collection.”

article_text:
Ella Maillart erkundete in den 1930er-Jahren als Reisende, Schriftstellerin und Fotografin zahlreiche Länder Asiens und hielt ihre Beobachtungen in Büchern und Fotografien fest. Nachdem ihr Nachlass in das Register des UNESCO-Weltdokumentenerbes aufgenommen wurde, widmet ihr das Photo Elysée diese Hommage.

Ella Maillart (1903–1997) war eine der aussergewöhnlichsten Schweizer Persönlichkeiten des 20. Jahrhunderts. Als unerschrockene Reisende, Fotografin, Journalistin und Sportlerin brach sie zeitlebens aus den engen gesellschaftlichen Konventionen ihrer Zeit aus. Ihr Werk umfasst faszinierende Fotografien und Reiseberichte aus dem 1930er Jahren, die heute als unschätzbare ethnografische Dokumente einer untergegangenen Epoche von hohem Informationswert sind.

Geboren am 20. Februar 1903 in Plainpalais (Genf), als Tochter eines wohlhabenden Pelzhändlers, begeisterte sich Maillart schon früh für die Natur und das Abenteuer. Sie war eine Pionierin des Frauen-Segelns, gründete den ersten Frauen-Hockeyclub der Westschweiz und vertrat die Schweiz – als einzige Frau – bei den Olympischen Spielen 1924 in Paris im Segeln im gesamten Wettbewerb. Zudem war sie eine exzellente Skifahrerin und startete mehrfach bei Weltmeisterschaften.

Dass Ella Maillart 1932 als Frau alleine in Sowjet-Zentralasien Kirgistan, Usbekistan und Kasachstan bereiste, um den harten Übergang der nomadischen Völker in die sowjetische Kollektivierung zu dokumentieren, zeugt von einem unbeschreiblichen Mut und einer grossen Abenteuerlust. Sie reiste oft unter extremen Bedingungen und mit minimalem Gepäck, wobei ihre Kamera ihre wichtigste Begleiterin war.

Damit noch nicht genug: 1935 durchquerte sie zusammen mit dem britischen Times-Journalisten Peter Fleming in einer siebenmonatigen, gefährlichen Reise verbotene Gebiete von Peking bis nach Kaschmir, was ihr die Veröffentlichung verschiedener Reiseberichte ermöglichte und sie international bekannt machte. 1939, am Vorabend des Zweiten Weltkriegs, brach sie zusammen mit der Schriftstellerin und Journalistin Annemarie Schwarzenbach per Auto von Genf über die Türkei und den Iran nach Kabul auf, wo Maillart zunächst ein unberührtes, friedliches Afghanistan dokumentierte.

Als die beiden Schweizerinnen in Kabul vom Ausbruch des Krieges erfuhren, trennten sich ihre Wege aufgrund der politischen Lage und Schwarzenbachs Drogenabhängigkeit. Während Schwarzenbach nach Europa zurückkehrte, reiste Maillart allein weiter nach Indien. Sie lebte überwiegend im Süden von Madras (heute Chennai) und unternahm von dort aus kürzere Reisen nach Tibet und Nepal. Die Kriegsjahre verbrachte sie in einem Ashram, wo sie sich intensiv mit hinduistischer Philosophie auseinandersetzte.

Ella Maillarts Fotografien zeichnen sich durch einen tiefen Humanismus aus. Sie war keine Touristin, die exotische Kulissen suchte, sondern eine teilnehmende Beobachterin. Ihre Porträts von Nomaden, Strassenverkäufern und Einheimischen zeugen von grossem Respekt, sowie von Empathie und Neugier auf Augenhöhe. Sie fing das alltägliche Leben ein, bevor die Globalisierung und politische Umwälzungen diese traditionellen Lebensweisen unwiderruflich veränderten.

Nach ihrer Rückkehr nach Europa liess sie sich im Walliser Bergdorf Chandolin nieder, wo sie bis zu ihrem Tod im Jahr 1997 lebte. Heute wird ihr umfangreiches Fotoarchiv vom Musée de l’Elysée in Lausanne und von der Fotostiftung Schweiz bewahrt und hält die Erinnerung an eine Frau wach, die Grenzen im Kopf und auf der Landkarte überwand.

Die gegenwärtige Ausstellung im Musée Elysée ist eine Hommage von internationaler Tragweite. Im Jahr 2025 wurde das Gesamtwerk von Ella Maillart offiziell von der UNESCO in das Weltdokumentenerbe («Memory of the World») aufgenommen. Da das Photo Elysée bereits seit 1988 ihren gigantischen fotografischen Nachlass aus mehreren tausend Bildern betreut, nutzt das Museum diesen Meilenstein für eine tiefgründige Aufarbeitung. Die schriftlichen Dokumente Maillarts sind in der Bibliotheque de Genève archiviert.

Die Qualität dieser Ausstellung zeichnet sich vor allem durch ein kluges kuratorisches Konzept aus. Statt einer reinen Aneinanderreihung von Bildern fokussiert sich die Schau auf den intensiven Dialog zwischen Bild und Text. Gezeigt werden die vier grossen Asienreisen der 1930er-Jahre (Sowjetunion, China, Iran und Afghanistan). Dabei macht die Ausstellung deutlich, dass Maillarts Arbeiten weit mehr als blosse Reisefotografie sind und sich durch einen unschätzbaren ethnografischen Wert auszeichnen. Die Besucher erleben hautnah mit, wie präzise sie die politischen und gesellschaftlichen Umbrüche jener Zeit – wie die sowjetische Kollektivierung Zentralasiens oder den Wandel Chinas – dokumentiert hat.

Die Arbeitsweise von Ella Maillart unterschied sie grundlegend von den klassischen Expeditionsfotografen jener Zeit, die mit grossen Plattenkameras umherzogen. Maillart hingegen hatte sich für die revolutionär leichte Leica-Kleinbildkamera entschieden, die ein extrem flexibles und schnelles Agieren ermöglichte, um damit unbemerkt in den Alltag der Menschen einzutauchen. Sie hielt so flüchtige Momente fest, die eine Geschichte erzählten, wobei die Porträtierten nahbar und lebendig wirken, da sie oft direkt und ungezwungen in die Kamera blicken.

Doch nicht nur die Kamera war ihr Werkzeug, sondern ebenso ihr Notizbuch. Sie verbrachte viel Zeit damit, ihre Bilder mit präzisen handschriftlichen Bildunterschriften, Kommentaren und Tagebucheinträgen zu versehen und führte später akribisch ein Archiv, bei dem jene Aufnahme eine Karteikarte erhielt, was in der Ausstellung in einem Raum visualisiert wird. Diese Symbiose aus Notizen und visueller Dokumentation ist der Grund, warum das Photo Elysée ihre Werke heute als «fotografische Erzählungen» präsentiert. Dabei liefert das Bild die Empathie und der Text die ethnografischen Fakten dazu.

Unter den extremen Bedingungen ihrer Expeditionen war der Umgang mit dem Fotomaterial für Ella Maillart ein logistischer und technischer Kraftakt. Hitze, Staub, Sand und die unabsehbare Länge der Reisen stellten Gefahren für das empfindliche Fotomaterial dar. Entgegen der Annahme, sie hätte alle Filme erst Monate später zu Hause entwickelt, entwickelte Maillart einen beachtlichen Teil ihrer Filme direkt während der Reise, um die Qualität zu prüfen und die Negative vor dem Verderben durch Hitze zu schützen. Sie führte einen extrem dichten Wechselsack mit, um darin die Filme blind in die Entwicklungsdosen einzuspulen. Das grösste Problem beim Entwickeln der Filme in Wüsten oder im afghanischen Sommer war die Wassertemperatur, da zu heisses Wasser zur Ablösung der Fotoemulsion vom Schichtträger bewirkte. Das nächste Problem war das Trocknen der Filme. In staubigen Wüsten oder Steppen musste dies im Inneren von Fahrzeugen oder in geschlossenen Lehmhütten erfolgen, damit ich keine Sandkörner auf der Schicht festsetzten. Filme, die sie nicht vor Ort entwickeln konnte, mussten monatelang unbeschadet über Tausende Kilometer transportiert werden, wozu sie verlötete oder speziell abgedichtete Blechdosen verwendete.

Der britische Journalist Peter Fleming, der Ella Maillart auf ihrer 6’000 Kilometer langen «Verbotenen Reise» von Peking nach Kaschmir im Jahr 1935 begleitete, hielt sich oft mit seinem typisch britischen, trockenen Humor über Maillarts Drang zum fotografischen Perfektionismus auf. Während er die Karawane vorwärtspeitschen wollte, stieg Maillart vom Kamel, um auf das richtige Licht zu warten oder ihren Standort zu optimieren. Oder Flming schildert in seinen Berichten die anscheinende Absurdität, wenn mitten in der Einöde Zentralasiens das Alltagsleben komplett stillstehen musste, weil Ella unter Decken kauerte, um Filme zu wechseln. Er taufte diese Prozeduren scherzhaft als ihre ganz eigenen rituellen Zeremonien, ohne die die Reise für sie nicht komplett gewesen wäre.

Trotz Flemings Frotzeleien machten Maillarts Bilder sein Buch «News from Tartary» erst zu dem visuellen Meisterwerk, als das es heute gilt. Es zeigt das faszinierende Zusammenspiel zweier völlig unterschiedlicher Reise- und Arbeitsstile.

Neben ihren Bildern hinterliess Ella Maillart zahlreiche Reisebücher (wie «Der bittere Weg» über die Reise mit Annemarie Schwarzenbach nach Afghanistan, «Ti-Puss» über ihre drei Jahre in Indien oder «Verbotene Reise» über die Reise mit Peter Fleming von Peking bis Kaschmir), die durch präzise Beobachtungsgabe und literarisches Geschick überzeugen. Die Bücher sind im Buchhandel oder im Shop des Musée Elysée erhältlich.

article_text:
A federal judge has temporarily blocked construction of President Donald Trump’s triumphal arch just hours after a hastily convened planning commission granted the project final approval.

U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan issued a restraining order Friday morning halting construction of the 250-foot arch for 14 days, giving the court time to consider lawsuits challenging the project’s legality. The order bans all activities related to the project, including excavation, utility installation, and road closures around its proposed located, Memorial Circle near Arlington Cemetery. The administration has been given a Monday, November 9, deadline to guarantee its compliance with the ruling.

The National Capital Planning Commission, composed mostly of Trump loyalists, approved the project on Thursday after a nine-hour virtual hearing in which more than 100 people testified, including military veterans, D.C. preservationists, and family members of those buried at Arlington. The outcome was widely expected, prompting opponents to seek federal court intervention before the review process had concluded. Their appeal succeeded: Judge Chutkan will consider several independent legal challenges to the arch, including one brought by the governments of D.C. and Virginia and another by Vietnam War veterans.

The lawsuits argue that the Trump administration bypassed the necessary congressional approval and failed to adequately assess the project’s potential impacts on the surrounding landscape. Critics have raised concerns about air and noise pollution, traffic disruptions, and other problems stemming from the structure’s height and location. They argue that the arch would interfere with flightpaths from DCA and, particularly controversially, disrupt the carefully cultivated visual relationship between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.

According to an October investigation by the Washington Post , which used a to-scale 3D model to map the arch’s shadows, the structure would cast shadows across more than 75,000 graves at Arlington over the course of the year, as well as several major memorials, including those dedicated to John F. Kennedy and Martin Luther King Jr., and the Vietnam Veterans and Korean War Veterans memorials.

The Trump administration has argued that the arch would serve as a necessary commemoration of the nation’s 250th anniversary of independence and enhance security in Washington, D.C. In recent weeks, Trump proposed that the structure could double as a “military complex” equipped for snipers and drones. The final plan submitted to the commission, however, reportedly omitted those details.

Mark Paoletta, a White House official and the commission’s chairman, called the empty space at Memorial Circle a “national disgrace” on Thursday and praised the president’s “historic vision.”

Construction is projected to take two to three years, with crews working nearly around the clock, according to the Trump administration.

article_text:
Dopo la conclusione di Homo Faber e della Venice Glass Week, è la Venice Design Week a innervare il tessuto urbano del capoluogo, che conferma un’attitudine ben precisa: la capacità di accogliere fermenti progettuali sempre nuovi con un’alta carica sperimentale. Nonostante i protagonisti di questa manifestazione provengano da ogni parte del mondo, il suo radicamento nella città lagunare è ben saldo e prolifico come quando, nei secoli passati, mercanti, intellettuali e artisti trovavano accoglienza soprattutto presso i palazzi aristocratici.

Secondo il genius veneziano , la Design Week, coordinata da Lisa Balasso , è inclusiva, incline al confronto. Stanze affrescate e androni accolgono linguaggi molto differenti tra loro, frutto a loro volta di precise scelte tecnologiche e costruttive. Pur rimanendo nella dimensione artigianale e dei pezzi unici, i diversi autori fanno evolvere tecniche produttive già note verso nuovi orizzonti tipologici e prestazionali.

Tra stampa 3D, acciaio e nuove forme dell’oggetto

Lo sa bene Marco De Gregorio , con la sua collezione di sedie stampate in 3D, soluzione esecutiva che permette di ottenere delle sagome e dei volumi mai raggiunti in precedenza e di espanderne la funzione come contenitore o come semplice effetto scultoreo.

Troviamo lo stesso approccio anche nel lavoro di Benjamin Böwing , giovane proveniente da Monaco di Baviera, che manipola le lastre d’acciaio in un virtuosismo costruttivo davvero unico. Tagli laser, assemblaggi precisissimi e torsioni trasformano attaccapanni, tavolini e sedute in oggetti davvero contemporanei, che strizzano l’occhio alla produzione di serie tipica della grande industria.

Nella stessa sede espositiva, ovvero la magnifica cornice dello studentato Combo, la lampada Nesuto esplora le possibilità di riflessione della luce su una texture ondulata. In questo caso fresatura e stampa 3D, che gestiscono la materia con tecniche chiaramente contrapposte, convergono in un medesimo risultato formale. Lo studio polacco – che a dispetto cella provenienza si chiama Bozzetti – la propone in vari formati e in due materiali molto diversi fra loro, ovvero il legno e la resina.

La luce protagonista a Palazzo Nani

Ma il lighting è il tema di un’esposizione specifica presso Palazzo Nani (Radisson Collection Hotel), il cui piano nobile ospita numerose proposte dal carattere intimista e lirico, quasi a voler confermare lo spirito poetico che permea tutta Venezia. Anche in questo caso, nuove tecnologie dialogano con un’artigianalità di alto livello, così come quest’ultima stabilisce un filo diretto con la Anisette di Vistosi, che invece è figlia di un’azienda storica e strutturata.

Questa sezione è forse quella che presenta il maggiore impatto e la maggiore coerenza nel quadro della Venice Design Week. Il soffitto affrescato del lounge settecentesco abbraccia una collezione pluralista e dinamica, in cui si riconosce la molteplicità di strade che connota il design contemporaneo, specie quello di matrice hand made. La stampa 3D, ancora una volta, domina le scelte produttive dei designer. Lo si vede nella splendida ONe da tavolo, espressiva e scintillante, creata da Fablab, ma anche nelle sfere organico-marine dell’armeno Leora, che sembrano uscite dai fondali lagunari.

La manualità, tuttavia, rivela un fascino intramontabile, come si evince dagli splendidi origami di Anita Cerpelloni oppure da Veilleur, la placca luminosa di Studio Hurt (dalla Francia), drammatica, un po’ brutalista, la cui matericità richiama alcuni quadri di Burri .

Una Venice Design Week 2026 per i giovani e l’autoproduzione

La VDW 2026 ci restituisce un quadro creativo ancora fortemente interessato alle giovani risorse del design. Anche questo aspetto decreta la peculiarità della manifestazione. Mentre le iniziative citate in apertura di articolo puntano su maestrie consolidate e di lungo corso, qui si punta sulla freschezza e sulla sperimentazione.

Il progetto veneziano perpetua ciò che accadeva negli eventi fuorisalone di Milano, “madre” di tutte le design week, scena di un design alternativo e “indipendente” (e soprattutto autoprodotto), prima che i grandi brand dell’arredo fagocitassero l’intera kermesse.

article_text:
Aamir Khan broke down onstage at the Singapore International Film Festival on Thursday as he recalled realizing, during the COVID-19 lockdown, that three decades of nonstop work had cost him years with his family.

The Bollywood superstar, who was handed the festival’s Screen Icon Award by Hong Kong director Peter Chan Ho-sun, also shed light on sequels to “3 Idiots” and “Andaz Apna Apna” during a wide-ranging in-conversation session moderated by Singapore comedian Rishi Budhrani.

Related Stories

‘Young Sheldon’ Star Iain Armitage Says the Show Was a ‘Big Undertaking’ as Co-Star Acknowledges He Could Be ‘Difficult’ to Work With

‘Young Sheldon’ Star Emily Osment Requested an Intimacy Coordinator Because of 'Uncomfortable' Age Gap With Montana Jordan: 'He Was a Baby!'

The emotional moment came late in the evening, when Khan was asked about the weakest point of his journey. He described himself as a lifelong workaholic who ate, slept and dreamed films, and said his family had always been understanding enough to leave him alone.

“When I was sitting in COVID and I was thinking, I said, you know, about 30 years have passed of my life. And it’s okay to work like a madman, completely obsessed with what you’re doing for one year, two years, five years. But if it goes on for 30 years, I mean, you’ve lost your relationships. Your kids have grown up, they’re adults now. So I felt a deep sense of loss,” Khan said.

He paused, broke down, apologized and gathered himself as the packed audience at the Grand Ballroom, Marina Bay Sands, broke into applause. An audience member handed the star a box of tissues.

Khan, wiping his tears away, said the experience pushed him to make a major change, and that for the last four years he has deliberately carved out time for his family and close friends. “I’m so glad that this thought occurred to me when I was 56 and not when I was 86, when it would be really too late to do anything about it,” he said.

On a lighter note, Khan was asked whether a sequel to “3 Idiots,” the 2009 campus comedy directed by Rajkumar Hirani, is in the works.

“Well, I’m not allowed to say a lot,” Khan said. “I think I can say this much, that yes, Raju is working on the script. In fact, hopefully once I’m back in the next couple of weeks, he’s going to narrate the final version to me. So, fingers crossed.”

According to Budhrani, Khan had phoned Hirani in front of him the previous day to check whether he could share the news, and the filmmaker gave his blessing – though Hirani didn’t pick up the first time, as Khan had changed his number. Khan said he had shut his phone a few weeks earlier and is now off all apps, having found that scrolling could swallow three hours at a stretch.

With many fans having shouted out their love for Rajkumar Santoshi’s 1994 cult comedy “Andaz Apna Apna,” Khan was asked whether a sequel is on the cards. “Well, I know that Raj Santoshi is working on something,” he said. “So let’s see what happens.” Asked if there was anything more, he replied: “Yeah, that’s all.”

In the same answer about his weakest moments, Khan recounted an earlier low point from the start of his career. After his 1988 debut “Qayamat Se Qayamat Tak” became a hit, he signed nine films within six months, reasoning that if established stars could juggle dozens of projects, he could handle 10. Once shooting began, he realized his mistake and would come home and weep to his then-wife Reena. The films then flopped one after another, and he was branded a “one-film wonder.”

“At that time, mentally and emotionally, I felt like I’m in quicksand. I’m sinking slowly, and the more I’m struggling to get out, the deeper I’m going,” Khan said.

At that point, Mahesh Bhatt, then riding high on “Saaransh,” “Arth” and “Naam,” offered him a film. Khan had vowed to commit only when he loved the script, the director and the producer, and he didn’t like the script. After a sleepless night, he turned Bhatt down. “If I had compromised with that and I had been practical, and I had, you know, said, ‘Yes, sir, I’m doing the film,’ I think my entire career would have been a series of compromises,” he said. They would go on to work together in “Dil Hai Ke Manta Nahin” and “Hum Hain Rahi Pyar Ke.”

Accepting the Screen Icon Award, Khan thanked the festival and said that having Chan present it made the moment special. “Filmmaking is a collective art form, and a lot of people contribute to each other’s work,” he said.

Asked why his films have resonated in China, Khan said “3 Idiots” took off there and across the wider region east of India after young viewers began passing it around, prompting them to seek out his other work. “I mean, it’s the truth. For me, my popularity in China is thanks to piracy,” he said, while stressing that he is not an advocate of it. He attributed the deeper connection to what he called a shared “emotional key” between Indian and Chinese audiences, recalling that watching “Dangal” in a Chinese theater felt like watching it in India.

Khan also revealed that he holds 50 to 60 test screenings of 25 people each for his films, and that the first test screening of “Taare Zameen Par” was a disaster. For smaller films whose budgets can’t absorb his usual fee, he said he skips the fee and takes a back end instead, so the producer is protected if the film doesn’t work.

On artificial intelligence, Khan said he views it as another filmmaking tool, much like VFX, and pointed to a castle set that would once have required 200 carpenters to build. “My common sense is telling me that in the short term, for sure, people are going to lose jobs,” he said.

Khan, who was last in Singapore nine years ago with “Secret Superstar,” also has a 25th anniversary screening of “Lagaan,” his first film as producer, lined up at the festival on Friday.

article_text:
W hat you expect from a film about a fancy high-end restaurant is a certain amount of heat: the roiling intensity of staff pushed to their absolute limits in the pursuit of gastronomic perfection. But this 1960s-set Peruvian drama instead maintains a gentle simmer, sedate and elegant. Perhaps it’s too elegant given the circumstances of its chef-proprietor, a high-society trophy wife with no catering experience who makes a high-stakes gamble on opening a successful restaurant.

Bárbara Mori is Norma, a glacial beauty who cultivates a kind of Jackie Onassis chic: huge sunglasses, massive blow-dry, makeup thickly applied like armour. One night, Norma’s husband humiliatingly leaves her for a beauty queen. You’d be sympathetic if Norma wasn’t so foul to the staff, lashing out at housekeeper Rosa (Hermelinda Luján) and chauffeur Oscar (Cesar Ballumbrosio). It’s Oscar (who is a bit in love with Norma) who suggests she opens a restaurant in the house to pay the mortgage. Norma’s father was the French ambassador to Peru, and she has picked up his passion for gastronomy. Although the script is a bit inconsistent on this, since Oscar also says he’s never seen her so much as light the oven.

The restaurant has four months to succeed before the bank repossesses the house. And still, there’s no sense of Norma, or the film, breaking into a sweat. She hires a Japanese Peruvian sous-chef in the kitchen; Oscar is front of house. But the early reviews are tepid, describing the French cuisine as a bit trad, and the restaurant is half empty. There are lessons to come about how teamwork makes the dream work, and embracing Peru’s cultural diversity. The trouble is that, before that, Norma is such an insufferable snob; it’s a bit too long to hold your nose and stick with her.

article_text:
After receiving rave reviews for his chilling portrayal of OpenAI guru Sam Altman, Andrew Garfield is headed towards a busy awards season and that now includes a prestigious new honor.

The Santa Barbara Film Festival on Tuesday said the two-time Oscar-nominated actor will receive the Maltin Modern Master Award at the fest’s 2027 edition. Garfield will join renowned film critic Leonard Maltin for an onstage conversation February 6 to reflect on his acclaimed career and wide-ranging body of work.

The honor comes on the heels of his latest performance in Luca Guadagnino’s Artificial , the story of OpenAI and a two-decade artificial intelligence arms race. The film recently premiered at the New York Film Festival to acclaim and will be released theatrically by Neon on Christmas Day.

“Andrew Garfield has long since proven himself to critics and audiences alike. It’s no simple matter to balance a career between mainstream Hollywood movies and challenging director-driven projects, but he has done exactly that and done it well,” said Maltin.

Watch on Deadline

The Modern Master Award was established in 1995. Created to honor an individual who has enriched the culture through accomplishments in the motion picture industry, it was re-named the Maltin Modern Master Award in 2015 in honor of longtime SBIFF moderator Maltin. Past recipients include last year’s Adam Sandler and Angelina Jolie, Jamie Lee Curtis, Nicole Kidman, Javier Bardem, Robert Downey Jr., Denzel Washington, Cate Blanchett, George Clooney, and Christopher Plummer, and acclaimed filmmakers including Christopher Nolan, James Cameron, Sean Penn, Clint Eastwood and Peter Jackson.

A two-time Academy Award nominee, Golden Globe and Tony Award winner, Garfield has established himself as one of the most versatile actors of his generation. He earned his first Oscar nomination for his portrayal of World War II medic Desmond Doss in Mel Gibson’s Hacksaw Ridge and his second for his performance as composer Jonathan Larson in Lin-Manuel Miranda’s Tick, Tick … Boom! for which he won the Golden Globe for Best Actor – Musical or Comedy. He also received a Golden Globe nom for David Fincher’s The Social Network .

Garfield’s credits include Martin Scorsese’s Silence , Ramin Bahrani’s 99 Homes , Mark Romanek’s Never Let Me Go , John Crowley’s We Live In Time opposite Florence Pugh and Guadagnino’s After The Hunt opposite Julia Roberts and Ayo Edebiri. He also brought Peter Parker to the screen in The Amazing Spider-Man films and reprised the role in Spider-Man: No Way Home . His most recent film, Paul Greengrass’ The Uprising, was released last month.

On TV, Garfield received an Emmy nomination for FX’s limited series Under the Banner of Heaven. His stage career includes a Tony-winning performance as Prior Walter in the Broadway revival of Tony Kushner’s Angels In America , as well as a Tony-nominated turn in Death of a Salesman . He will next appear opposite Jude Law in the Apple TV limited series Wild Things about Siegfried & Roy.

The 42nd Santa Barbara Film Festival will run February 3-11, 2027.

editorial_excerpt_zh: 本次展览介绍被称为“印象派先驱”、“印象派之父”的19世纪法国画家尤金·布丹（1824-1898）的绘画生涯。布丹以清新色彩和轻快笔触描绘故乡诺曼底的天空、海景和牧场中的牛群而闻名。他在户外直接观察自然，描绘易变的光线和大气，这种创作手法对年轻的克劳德·莫奈等当时画家产生了巨大影响，最终促成了印象派的诞生。特别是他对天空和云朵的描绘，被诗人波德莱尔评价为“气象学的美”，并受到巴比松画派画家柯罗“天空之王”的赞誉。此次展览是日本30年来首次大规模的布丹作品展，将聚焦人物和建筑主题，通过约100件油画、素描、粉彩和版画作品，从新视角重新审视布丹对现代风景画发展的巨大贡献。

本展は、「印象派の先駆者」「印象派の父」と呼ばれる19世紀フランスの画家ウジェーヌ・ブーダン（1824-1898）の画業を紹介する展覧会です。ブーダンは故郷ノルマンディーの空、海景、牧場の牛などをみずみずしい色彩と軽快な筆運びで表現したことで知られます。戸外で自然をじかに観察しながら、うつろいやすい光や大気を描写する制作手法は、若きクロード・モネをはじめとする当時の画家たちに大きな影響を与え、やがて印象派の誕生につながっていきます。特に空や雲の表現は詩人ボードレールに「気象学的美の世界」と評され、バルビゾン派の画家コローに「空の王者」と称賛されています。 日本では30年ぶりの本格的な展覧会となる今回は、人物や建築モチーフなどにも焦点を当てつつ、油彩、素描、パステル、版画などの約100点の作品により近代風景画の発展に大きく寄与したブーダンの魅力を新たな視点で問い直します。

article_text:
A Nazi-looted painting that once belonged to a Dutch Jewish family, and at one point hung in Adolf Hitler’s home, has been traced in new research, the Dutch newspaper Het Parool reports.

The work in question is German painter Carl Gottlieb Peschel’s Joseph Sold by His Brothers (1831), which shows the biblical scene of Joseph being sold into slavery in Egypt.

The painting belonged to Bob Nijkerk, whose family had made its fortune in the iron and scrap-metal business in the 19th century. Nijkerk, who died in 1987, used that wealth to build a collection of bibliophile editions, modern Dutch typography, and paintings. He received the Peschel as a gift from his brother-in-law in 1941. When the Nazis occupied Amsterdam in 1940, he was a managing director of the family company, which the Nazis seized in 1941.

Starting in 1942, the Nazis deported more than 100,000 Dutch Jews to killing centers. Nijkerk, his wife, and their three children were spared at first. Willem Sandberg, a curator at Amsterdam’s Stedelijk Museum, where Nijkerk had loaned and donated artworks, intervened on their behalf and got them placed on an exception list of about 700 Jews. In 1940 the two men visited the museum’s art bunker together, and the collector likely stored important works there.

The family was first taken to De Schaffelaar Castle, about 45 minutes outside Amsterdam. They were later deported to the Westerbork camp in the Netherlands and then to Theresienstadt in what is now the Czech Republic. “Ultimately, all five survived the war because they were brought to Switzerland by train in 1945 along with a select group of camp prisoners from Theresienstadt,” Het Parool reports. Nijkerk’s grandson Willem Nijkerk knew that his family had included bibliophiles but didn’t know how large his grandfather’s collection was. He learned of the family’s link to the painting from Diederik Oostdijk, a professor of English and American literature at the Vrije Universiteit in Amsterdam.

“I mainly knew about the period during and after the war. Through Oostdijk’s research, I was given a glimpse into their prewar life. They lived in relatively grand luxury,” Willem told Het Parool .

Oostdijk tells the Nijkerk family’s story in his new book, Overlevingskunst (The Art of Survival). According to its description, the book follows “three Jewish families [who] miraculously escaped the Holocaust thanks to their art collections.”

Oostdijk’s research shows that the Peschel spent some time in Hitler’s Berlin home. It was then moved to Hitler’s storage facility in Munich, where prized works were held for a planned Führermuseum.

It is still unclear whether Bob Nijkerk sold the painting in late 1941 or early 1942, or whether it was confiscated later, when German forces or their Dutch collaborators raided Jewish homes. After the war, Nijkerk recovered many of his books but “never uttered a word about Peschel’s painting,” Willem said. “I don’t think he had much of a connection to the painting himself. The painting does not evoke much emotion in me either.”

Nijkerk’s seven descendants have not filed a formal restitution claim for the Peschel. They also have not claimed three other paintings that Oostdijk has linked to the Nijkerk collection: two 1633 portraits by Caspar Netscher and a 1673 painting by Gerbrand van den Eeckhout. Those three works are at the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam. Joseph Sold by His Brothers is now in the Martin von Wagner Museum in Würzburg, Germany. Willem said that if the paintings are ever restituted, the family would likely sell them.

“It is a bizarre thought that a painting belonging to my grandparents was in Hitler’s residence, one of the most horrific human beings who ever lived, and to think that he found this work so beautiful,” Willem told Het Parool . “I don’t necessarily want Peschel’s painting on my wall at home. I also find it an unpleasant thought that it lay in Hitler’s home.”

What was the dynamic like between the five girls behind the scenes on The Virgin Suicides ? For instance, which girls were the closest, who was the loudest, who was the quietest, etc? Imogen067 Their personalities did kind of emerge. We did rehearsals where we all hung out together and had them interact as a family and they cooked together. They hung out off set and they started to bond. Chelse Swain was the most eccentric one.

The postmodern soundtrack in Marie Antoinette, all that post-punk and new romantic music, was so audacious that it took your film to a staggering level of artistry. What was the original idea behind bringing those two worlds together? Dmitry_S When I first started reading about Marie Antoinette in Antonia Fraser’s book, I was struck by how young she was. She was 14 when she came to Versailles and around 18 when she became queen. So I really wanted to convey that she and Louis were teenagers, and I thought back to the new romantic music I was listening to when I was a teenager. I was lucky that I had a big brother who exposed me to good music at a young age. I wanted to show it through that filter of Bow Wow Wow and Adam Ant. When the film came out, some people were offended because it just wasn’t usual to put contemporary music in a period film.

Your 2003 video for the White Stripes’ cover of I Just Don’t Know What to Do With Myself has been rated by Rolling Stone as one of the sexiest music videos ever . What other ideas were considered before you landed on Kate Moss pole dancing for three minutes? McScootikins Oh, wow, I didn’t know that. That’s so cool. I don’t know where it came from. It was just my idea, and I was glad that everyone was on board with it. I just asked Kate to do that, she said yes, and the band was into it.

Are you aware that you’re a girlblogger icon? sleepy_nym I don’t know that much about bloggers, but that’s nice to hear. I’ll have to ask my teenage daughters. I do appreciate that my work was made a while ago, so it’s great that it connects with young women of this generation.

What was it like working on Tim Burton’s 1984 short film Frankenweenie , before Tim Burton was “Tim Burton”? jasonaparkes That was such a fun experience. I was 12 or something. I think Tim Burton was right out of school. It was an early short film, so it was really fun to meet him and be on his set – he used to do drawings for me. I’d spent a lot of time on my dad’s film sets, so it was fun to be on someone else’s. I still like to visit film sets. I’m never jaded – I’m still impressed by movie magic.

Didn’t you mind having your mum filming behind the scenes for all those hours when you were making Marie Antoinette? Dr_J_A_Zoidberg My mom always had a grounding mom presence. It was a stressful shoot, so it was nice to have her there. She also appreciated all the beauty of the costumes and the details of the food and the flowers, so it was fun to show it to her, and she was really into filming all the details and how it was made. I forgot about the footage until recently and I didn’t realise how much there was. My mom had almost 80 hours of footage, so it was a real treat to have this home movie to revisit. I never thought we would do something with it.

You’re not going to answer this – but someone has to ask it anyway. What does Bob whisper to Charlotte at the end of Lost in Translation ? rolleyes I like what Bill [Murray] always says. He says, “It’s between them,” so I’ll leave it at that.

article_text:
Il piacere di cercare un capo fuori produzione, trovare un disco che mancava alla propria raccolta, o ancora imbattersi in un libro dall’edizione ormai fuori produzione: anche questo passa dai mercatini. Tra abbigliamento second hand, accessori, design e collezionismo, il fine settimana del 24 e 25 ottobre offre diverse occasioni per curiosare tra proposte che difficilmente si incontrano nei circuiti commerciali tradizionali, con appuntamenti che si distribuiscono tra Emilia-Romagna, Toscana, Lombardia e Lazio. Ecco alcuni mercatini da segnare in agenda per il fine settimana.

Firenze: East Market alla Manifattura Tabacchi

Sabato 24 e domenica 25 ottobre East Market torna nuovamente a Firenze presso MOTEL, il nuovo spazio eventi della Manifattura Tabacchi. Per questa seconda edizione toscana sono annunciati oltre cento espositori provenienti da tutta Italia e una selezione che attraversa abbigliamento vintage e second hand, streetwear, accessori, vinili, design e oggetti da collezione. La proposta comprende capi dagli anni Cinquanta ai Duemila, insieme a pezzi di modernariato, libri, stampe e curiosità.

Il market, attivo a Milano dal 2014, era arrivato nella capitale fiorentina per la prima volta nel mese di maggio di quest’anno, con il suo motto « Everything Old Is New Again ». Tra gli espositori il napoletano Raffaele Iorio , collezionista di occhiali vintage con modelli rari firmati Versace, Dior, Fendi, Ray-Ban e Persol; da Milano Spaghettochild Research specializzato in capi anni ’80 e ’90 e cultura skate; e Barbara Gosi , da Firenze, con pubblicità vintage originali dagli anni ’20 agli anni ’90. Anche questa volta sarà presente l’area musica curata da Fabio Rossi , con vinili e CD, prime stampe e rarità che spaziano dal rock al jazz, dall’elettronica all’hip-hop. Durante la manifestazione, la sala cinema di Manifattura Tabacchi ospiterà poi East TV , un percorso attraverso la storia dei videoclip musicali, con proiezioni gratuite a ciclo continuo. In programma video iconici come Thriller di Michael Jackson , …Baby One More Time di Britney Spears e Hey Ya! degli Outkast . Infine Bar Ventura, ispirato ai locali italiani degli anni Settanta, Ottanta e Novanta, insieme ai bar e agli spazi dedicati alla gastronomia già presenti negli spazi di Manifattura Tabacchi.

L’evento è aperto sabato dalle 10 alle 23 e domenica dalle 10 alle 21.

Forlì: la Fiera del Vintage

Dal 23 al 25 ottobre torna a Forlì Vintage! La moda che vive due volte , organizzata da Romagna Fiere con la direzione tecnica e artistica di Simone Velleca . La manifestazione riunisce diverse aree dedicate alla moda e agli oggetti del Novecento, dall’abbigliamento agli accessori, passando per il modernariato, il design e il collezionismo. Accanto ai capi d’epoca, l’area dedicata al fashion remake guarda al recupero creativo dei materiali e alla rielaborazione di forme e stili del passato, con un percorso che comprende anche vinili, memorabilia e oggetti da collezione. La novità di quest’anno sarà Collezionare , un’area dedicata alla cultura pop, alla memoria e alle passioni intergenerazionali, in un un percorso che va dai primi anni Duemila agli anni Novanta.

La fiera apre venerdì 23 ottobre dalle 14 alle 20 e prosegue sabato 24 e domenica 25, dalle 10 alle 20.

Roma: Remira Market a Trastevere e Ficus al Massimo

Dopo il Monk e il Maxxi , domenica 25 ottobre il market di Remira – da settembre approdato a Trastevere – torna negli spazi di Zalib, in via della Penitenza 35. Il market riunisce circa quaranta espositori provenienti da diverse parti d’Italia, tra abbigliamento vintage, accessori, design, artigianato e pezzi unici. «Una cosa non è mai cambiata: la voglia di creare un luogo dove il vintage diventa incontro, scoperta e condivisione», così Remira Market annunciava il mese scorso la sua nuova sede.

Il pubblico potrà vivere una giornata di shopping sostenibile integrata ad attività culturali, spazi lettura e momenti di socialità nel verde, guardando anche alle radici del luogo e alla storica libreria di Via della Gatta, salvata nel 2017 da una mobilitazione cittadina, oggi vivace centro culturale che tra il 2020 e il 2024 ha promosso quasi 600 iniziative tra concerti, cinema e mostre. Si incontrano quindi il mercato e la libreria indipendente, in uno spazio che guarda alla cultura del riuso da prospettive differenti.

L’appuntamento è gratuito, previa registrazione, e il mercato è aperto dalle 10:30 alle 19.

Visualizza questo post su Instagram Un post condiviso da Remira Market • Roma vintage (@remira_roma)

Sempre a Roma, sabato 24 e domenica 25 ottobre il Garum – Museo della Cucina , in via dei Cerchi 87, ospita una nuova edizione di Ficus al Massimo . Il market occuperà le sale del museo, che custodisce una notevole collezione dedicata alla storia della cucina, e la corte esterna, con una proposta che comprenderà abbigliamento, pezzi vintage, gioielli, ceramiche, illustrazioni, complementi d’arredo e produzioni artigianali. Tra i progetti annunciati figurano realtà che lavorano sulla personalizzazione dei capi e sul recupero dei tessuti, affiancate da illustratori e designer indipendenti. Il pubblico potrà entrare in contatto con artigiani e creativi, conoscendo le storie dietro le loro opere e scegliendo oggetti difficili da trovare nei tradizionali circuiti commerciali.

L’appuntamento prevede in entrambe le giornate un’apertura dalle 10:30 alle 20, con ingresso gratuito.

Milano: BAD MARKET alla Bovisa

Sabato 24 ottobre il Circolo Bovisa ospita a Milano la prima edizione di BAD MARKET, un nuovo appuntamento dedicato al vintage, al modernariato, ai gioielli autoprodotti e alla creatività indipendente. La formula usa come filo conduttore la creatività e mette insieme la ricerca tra gli oggetti e una dimensione più conviviale, con l’intenzione di creare un appuntamento che possa tornare anche nelle prossime settimane. Per questa prima edizione, l’attenzione è rivolta a chi cerca accessori, pezzi d’arredo e proposte artigianali al di fuori della distribuzione tradizionale.

Il mercato si svolgerà alla Bovisa, in via Luigi Mercantini 11, dalle 14 alle 21, con musica dal vivo a partire dalle 19.

Valmadrera: il Vintage Market sul lago di Lecco

Domenica 25 ottobre torna il Valmadrera Vintage Market, nel piazzale del mercato di via Molini, in provincia di Lecco . L’appuntamento, attivo dal 2013, riunisce espositori, collezionisti e creativi con proposte che spaziano dagli oggetti vintage ai pezzi da collezione, fino all’artigianato. «Vogliamo che chi visita il Valmadrera Vintage Market abbia sempre la sensazione che possa esserci qualcosa da scoprire dietro l’angolo. Non soltanto acquistare, ma curiosare, riconoscere un oggetto del passato, lasciarsi sorprendere e magari tornare a casa con qualcosa che pochi minuti prima non stava nemmeno cercando» spiega Moris Sandionigi , presidente dell’Ufficio Gestione Turismo di Valmadrera, l’associazione organizzatrice della manifestazione

Il mercato è aperto dalle 8:30 alle 17 e prevede un’area street food. La posizione, a breve distanza dal lago e dai percorsi naturalistici della zona, permette di abbinare la visita alle bancarelle a una passeggiata nei dintorni.

article_text:
Produção estava paralizada para que o diretor pudesse se dedicar a uma questão familiar.

Com Matt Reeves afastado para cuidar de assuntos familiares, a direção de “ Batman: Parte II ” ganhou um reforço inesperado. Steven Soderbergh vai assumir o comando das gravações até o final, com Reeves retornando para a etapa de pós-produção do novo filme assim que estiver pronto. (via Deadline ).

Soderbergh é um admirador de longa data do trabalho de Reeves e, como Reeves não pôde estar no set, o diretor vencedor do Oscar se ofereceu para ajudar a concluir as filmagens principais. Reeves precisou se ausentar da produção desde o início de outubro, o que levou as gravações a serem paralizadas. A solução com Soderbergh vem para que o calendário de divulgação de “Batman: Parte II” não precise ser prolongado, e os dois trabalharão juntos e manterão contato até o término das filmagens.

A DC Studios divulgou um comunicado a respeito da entrada de Soderbergh no projeto:

“Como Matt Reeves continua lidando com uma questão familiar, Steven Soderbergh — um admirador do trabalho de Matt — entrou em contato com ele e assumirá a função, com total apoio da DC Studios, para ajudar o roteirista e diretor a concluir as últimas semanas das filmagens principais de ‘Batman Part 2’. Matt e Steven trabalharão em estreita colaboração com o elenco e a equipe técnica para concretizar a visão de Matt para o filme.”

Soderbergh também divulgou um comunicado:

“Achei o trabalho de Matt Reeves em ‘Batman’ impressionante; foi algo intencional, específico e rigorosamente coerente. O objetivo aqui é trabalhar com Matt e sua equipe para produzir material que se integre perfeitamente ao que já foi filmado, permitindo que Matt conclua seu filme da maneira adequada.”

Por fim, Reeves confirmou através de suas redes sociais que não está deixando a produção e que retornará assim que puder.

Just to be clear, I am not leaving The Batman Part II. I am profoundly grateful to Steven for coming to my aid during this challenging time to help me finish principal photography. Thank you to all for your concern and well wishes. 🦇 — Matt Reeves (@mattreevesLA) October 15, 2026

“Para deixar claro: não estou saindo de ‘Batman: Parte II’. Sou profundamente grato ao Steven por ter vindo me ajudar durante este período desafiador, auxiliando-me a concluir as filmagens principais. Obrigado a todos pela preocupação e pelos votos de melhoras. 🦇”

O novo filme continua a história do Batman vivido por Robert Pattinson, que fez sua estreia nos cinemas em 2022. Além de Pattinson, o elenco conta também com os retornos de Colin Farrell como Pinguim, Andy Serkis como Alfred, Jeffrey Wright como o Comissário James Gordon, Jayme Lawson como a prefeita Bella Réal e Gil Perez-Abraham como o policial Martínez. Novos nomes incluem Sebastian Stan, Scarlett Johansson, Charles Dance, Brian Tyree Henry e Sebastian Koch. Matt Reeves assina o roteiro junto a Mattson Tomlin.

A princípio, a estreia de “Batman: Parte II” segue mantida para 18 de fevereiro de 2028.

"text": "我们在 Fotointern.ch 上评论一本法语书籍，这又是一次打破常规的做法。通过这篇文章，我们希望让更多人了解安德烈·施密特及其作品。在130多年前，他主要在瑞士西部以及国外从事摄影活动，留下了大量迄今鲜为人知的遗作。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当安德烈·施密特于1836年出生时，摄影术仍然是少数先驱者的专利。在他三岁时，法国政府向全球公众介绍了达盖尔银版摄影法。在完成刺绣图案设计师的学徒培训后，施密特在湿版火棉胶工艺在很大程度上取代达盖尔银版摄影法之际，通过自学掌握了摄影。24岁时，他在洛桑圣洛朗街19号开设了一家照相馆，8年后搬到了大桥街（Grand-Pont），并于1878年在伊韦尔东定居。1885年后，他前往法国、阿尔及利亚和奥地利进行了多次旅行，并用镜头记录了下来。自1895年起，他开始深入研究X射线摄影和天体摄影，并为此发表了多篇文章。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "该书还让我们得以一窥其摄影遗作整理工作的趣闻。约2500张火棉胶底片以及少量的明胶银盐底片在“洛桑数字化工作室”（Atelier de numérisation de "施密特的摄影创作异常多元。其核心是肖像画、名片照（Cartes-de-visite）以及洛桑及其周边的风光。尤其是城市景观，如今已成为珍贵的时代文献，展示了沃州大都市在19世纪末期发展的迅猛势头。他大画幅的摄影作品至今仍以其卓越的画质令人印象深刻，并证明了他的摄影造诣与手工技艺。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": Dabei erweist sich der reich illustrierte Katalog als weit mehr als eine Begleitpublikation: Er ist ein wichtiges Dokument zur Schweizer Fotografiegeschichte."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Dass wir auf Fotointern.ch ein französischsprachiges Buch besprechen, ist einmal mehr eine Ausnahme von der Regel. Mit diesem Beitrag möchten wir André Schmid und sein Werk bekannter machen. Er war vor mehr als 130 Jahren vor allem in der Westschweiz, aber auch im Ausland fotografisch tätig und hinterliess einen umfangreichen, bisher wenig bekannten Nachlass."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Als André Schmid 1836 zur Welt kam, war die Fotografie noch wenigen Pionieren vorbehalten. Als er drei Jahre alt war, wurde die Daguerreotypie von der französischen Regierung der Weltöffentlichkeit vorgestellt. Nach einer Lehre als Stickmusterzeichner befasste sich Schmid autodidaktisch mit der Fotografie, als das nasse Kollodiumverfahren die Daguerreotypie weitgehend verdrängt hatte. Mit 24 eröffnete er in Lausanne ein Atelier an der Rue Saint-Laurent 19, zog acht Jahre später an den Grand-Pont und liess sich 1878 in Yverdon nieder. Nach 1885 führten ihn verschiedene Reisen nach Frankreich, Algerien und Österreich, die er fotografisch dokumentierte. Ab 1895 beschäftigte er sich intensiv mit der Röntgen- und Astrofotografie und veröffentlichte dazu mehrere Artikel."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Das Buch vermittelt auch einen interessanten Einblick in die Aufarbeitung seines fotografischen Nachlasses. Rund 2500 Kollodiumplatten sowie eine kleinere Anzahl Silbergelatineplatten wurden im «Atelier de numérisation de Lausanne» digitalisiert, um die Originale anschliessend fachgerecht restaurieren und archivieren zu können. Zum Bestand gehören zudem etwa 6000 Albuminabzüge, die sich teilweise in sehr schlechtem Zustand befinden und von denen nur die wichtigsten restauratorisch bearbeitet werden konnten. Damit dokumentiert das Buch auch die aufwendige Arbeit zur Bewahrung eines bedeutenden fotografischen Erbes."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Schmids fotografisches Schaffen war ausserordentlich vielseitig. Den Schwerpunkt bildeten Porträts, Cartes-de-visite-Bilder sowie Ansichten von Lausanne und Umgebung. Besonders die Stadtansichten sind heute wertvolle Zeitdokumente, die zeigen, wie rasant sich die Waadtländer Metropole gegen Ende des 19. Jahrhunderts entwickelte. Seine grossformatigen Aufnahmen beeindrucken noch heute durch ihre hervorragende Bildqualität und zeugen von seinem fotografischen Können und handwerklichen Geschick."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Neben den kommerziellen Arbeiten umfasst sein Nachlass zahlreiche Familienbilder, darunter Porträts seiner Frau Joséphine, seines Sohnes Alfred (geboren 1870) und vor allem seiner Enkelin Irène, deren Heranwachsen er während anderthalb Jahrzehnten fotografisch begleitete. Gerade diese persönlichen Aufnahmen gehören wohl zu seinen aussagestärksten Porträts. Sie zeigen eine andere, intimere Seite seines Schaffens, die über die Konventionen der damaligen Atelierfotografie hinausgeht."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Ergänzt wird das Buch durch drei Portfolios zeitgenössischer Fotoschaffender aus dem Umfeld der Lausanner Kunsthochschule ECAL: Olivier Jeannin («Ek-stase»), Léonore Baud («Les arbres nus») sowie Arbeiten von Absolventinnen und Absolventen («ECAL after Schmid»). Sie schaffen einen interessanten Dialog zwischen Vergangenheit und Gegenwart und setzen sich auf unterschiedliche Weise mit dem historischen Werk auseinander."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Für wen ist dieses Buch? Obwohl als Ausstellungskatalog konzipiert, spricht «Photo-sensible» einen weit grösseren Interessentenkreis an als nur die Ausstellungsbesuchenden. Besonders für fotogeschichtlich Interessierte ist es eine lohnende Entdeckung. Mit seinen zahlreichen bisher kaum bekannten Bildern ist das Buch zugleich eine wertvolle Dokumentation der Kollodiumfotografie und ein faszinierendes Zeugnis des Stadtbildes und gesellschaftlichen Lebens im Lausanne des ausgehenden 19. Jahrhunderts. Damit besitzt es einen bleibenden Wert, der weit über die Dauer der Ausstellung hinausreicht."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Urs Tillmanns"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Buchbeschreibung des Verlages"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Im Zeitalter digital erzeugter und gespeicherter Bilder üben analoge Verfahren zum Abbilden und Festhalten von Dingen, Ereignissen und Eindrücken eine grosse, zuweilen nostalgische Anziehungskraft aus. Tausende Glasnegative des Fotografen André Schmid (1836–1914), der in Lausanne eines der ersten kommerziellen Fotoateliers der Stadt betrieb, bilden ein faszinierendes Erbe. Seine Aufnahmen bieten Einblicke in die Gesellschaft und deren Normen im späten 19. und frühen 20. Jahrhundert. Mit ihrer rohen, handwerklichen Ausdruckskraft und einer von zahlreichen Gebrauchsspuren hervorgehobenen Materialität entfalten die Negative eine besondere Ästhetik, die Realismus, Vergänglichkeit und Poesie verbindet."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Photo-sensible gewährt Einblicke in den Nachlass André Schmids, wobei zahlreiche seiner Glasnegative durch den Abdruck in diesem Buch erstmals Bildstatus erlangen. Diesem authentischen Fenster in die Vergangenheit gegenüber stehen die Blicke der zeitgenössischen Fotokünstler/innen Léonore Baud und Olivier Jeannin sowie von Absolvent/innen der Fotografie-Klasse der École cantonale d’art de Lausanne (ECAL), die durch ihre Arbeiten das sinnliche Potenzial der historischen Aufnahmen von André Schmid hervorheben."}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Der Inhalt"}, article_text:
Das Historische Museum Lausanne zeigt derzeit eine Ausstellung über den in der Deutschschweiz kaum bekannten Fotografen André Schmid (1836–1914). Dabei erweist sich der reich illustrierte Katalog als weit mehr als eine Begleitpublikation: Er ist ein wichtiges Dokument zur Schweizer Fotografiegeschichte.

Dass wir auf Fotointern.ch ein französischsprachiges Buch besprechen, ist einmal mehr eine Ausnahme von der Regel. Mit diesem Beitrag möchten wir André Schmid und sein Werk bekannter machen. Er war vor mehr als 130 Jahren vor allem in der Westschweiz, aber auch im Ausland fotografisch tätig und hinterliess einen umfangreichen, bisher wenig bekannten Nachlass.

Als André Schmid 1836 zur Welt kam, war die Fotografie noch wenigen Pionieren vorbehalten. Als er drei Jahre alt war, wurde die Daguerreotypie von der französischen Regierung der Weltöffentlichkeit vorgestellt. Nach einer Lehre als Stickmusterzeichner befasste sich Schmid autodidaktisch mit der Fotografie, als das nasse Kollodiumverfahren die Daguerreotypie weitgehend verdrängt hatte. Mit 24 eröffnete er in Lausanne ein Atelier an der Rue Saint-Laurent 19, zog acht Jahre später an den Grand-Pont und liess sich 1878 in Yverdon nieder. Nach 1885 führten ihn verschiedene Reisen nach Frankreich, Algerien und Österreich, die er fotografisch dokumentierte. Ab 1895 beschäftigte er sich intensiv mit der Röntgen- und Astrofotografie und veröffentlichte dazu mehrere Artikel.

Das Buch vermittelt auch einen interessanten Einblick in die Aufarbeitung seines fotografischen Nachlasses. Rund 2500 Kollodiumplatten sowie eine kleinere Anzahl Silbergelatineplatten wurden im «Atelier de numérisation de Lausanne» digitalisiert, um die Originale anschliessend fachgerecht restaurieren und archivieren zu können. Zum Bestand gehören zudem etwa 6000 Albuminabzüge, die sich teilweise in sehr schlechtem Zustand befinden und von denen nur die wichtigsten restauratorisch bearbeitet werden konnten. Damit dokumentiert das Buch auch die aufwendige Arbeit zur Bewahrung eines bedeutenden fotografischen Erbes.

Schmids fotografisches Schaffen war ausserordentlich vielseitig. Den Schwerpunkt bildeten Porträts, Cartes-de-visite-Bilder sowie Ansichten von Lausanne und Umgebung. Besonders die Stadtansichten sind heute wertvolle Zeitdokumente, die zeigen, wie rasant sich die Waadtländer Metropole gegen Ende des 19. Jahrhunderts entwickelte. Seine grossformatigen Aufnahmen beeindrucken noch heute durch ihre hervorragende Bildqualität und zeugen von seinem fotografischen Können und handwerklichen Geschick.

Neben den kommerziellen Arbeiten umfasst sein Nachlass zahlreiche Familienbilder, darunter Porträts seiner Frau Joséphine, seines Sohnes Alfred (geboren 1870) und vor allem seiner Enkelin Irène, deren Heranwachsen er während anderthalb Jahrzehnten fotografisch begleitete. Gerade diese persönlichen Aufnahmen gehören wohl zu seinen aussagestärksten Porträts. Sie zeigen eine andere, intimere Seite seines Schaffens, die über die Konventionen der damaligen Atelierfotografie hinausgeht.

Ergänzt wird das Buch durch drei Portfolios zeitgenössischer Fotoschaffender aus dem Umfeld der Lausanner Kunsthochschule ECAL: Olivier Jeannin («Ek-stase»), Léonore Baud («Les arbres nus») sowie Arbeiten von Absolventinnen und Absolventen («ECAL after Schmid»). Sie schaffen einen interessanten Dialog zwischen Vergangenheit und Gegenwart und setzen sich auf unterschiedliche Weise mit dem historischen Werk auseinander.

Für wen ist dieses Buch? Obwohl als Ausstellungskatalog konzipiert, spricht «Photo-sensible» einen weit grösseren Interessentenkreis an als nur die Ausstellungsbesuchenden. Besonders für fotogeschichtlich Interessierte ist es eine lohnende Entdeckung. Mit seinen zahlreichen bisher kaum bekannten Bildern ist das Buch zugleich eine wertvolle Dokumentation der Kollodiumfotografie und ein faszinierendes Zeugnis des Stadtbildes und gesellschaftlichen Lebens im Lausanne des ausgehenden 19. Jahrhunderts. Damit besitzt es einen bleibenden Wert, der weit über die Dauer der Ausstellung hinausreicht.

Urs Tillmanns

Buchbeschreibung des Verlages

Im Zeitalter digital erzeugter und gespeicherter Bilder üben analoge Verfahren zum Abbilden und Festhalten von Dingen, Ereignissen und Eindrücken eine grosse, zuweilen nostalgische Anziehungskraft aus. Tausende Glasnegative des Fotografen André Schmid (1836–1914), der in Lausanne eines der ersten kommerziellen Fotoateliers der Stadt betrieb, bilden ein faszinierendes Erbe. Seine Aufnahmen bieten Einblicke in die Gesellschaft und deren Normen im späten 19. und frühen 20. Jahrhundert. Mit ihrer rohen, handwerklichen Ausdruckskraft und einer von zahlreichen Gebrauchsspuren hervorgehobenen Materialität entfalten die Negative eine besondere Ästhetik, die Realismus, Vergänglichkeit und Poesie verbindet.

Photo-sensible gewährt Einblicke in den Nachlass André Schmids, wobei zahlreiche seiner Glasnegative durch den Abdruck in diesem Buch erstmals Bildstatus erlangen. Diesem authentischen Fenster in die Vergangenheit gegenüber stehen die Blicke der zeitgenössischen Fotokünstler/innen Léonore Baud und Olivier Jeannin sowie von Absolvent/innen der Fotografie-Klasse der École cantonale d’art de Lausanne (ECAL), die durch ihre Arbeiten das sinnliche Potenzial der historischen Aufnahmen von André Schmid hervorheben.
